title: The Truth about Relativity
hook: A useless middle choice can make the larger bill feel like the only sensible one.
counterintuition: The option that changes your mind may be the one nobody is meant to choose. A decoy wins by losing clearly, so the favored option can borrow its glow.
tryThisNow: Cover the option that mainly makes another option look good, then ask whether the apparent winner still solves the original need.
keyTakeaway: Before choosing, test the comparison frame; a clear winner inside the wrong frame can still be the wrong choice.

breakdown.fastRead:
The membership sheet looks helpful because it gives you three choices. Basic, supporter, patron. Then you notice the supporter tier costs nearly as much as patron but has none of the lounge access, guest passes, or early-entry perks. Suddenly patron looks disciplined, even if you walked in wanting two family visits and a parking discount.

Relativity is useful until someone arranges the nearby benchmark for you. The weak option does not need buyers. It only needs to make another option look dominant.

Cover the loser and rebuild the choice around use.
breakdown.deepRead:
The Economist once offered a web subscription, a print subscription, and a web-plus-print bundle. The print-only price sat beside the bundle like a doomed contestant. It did not have to sell. Its job was to make the bundle look like the obvious bargain, and once it disappeared, many choices shifted.

That is the decoy effect in plain clothes. You are not measuring absolute value. You are comparing what is easy to compare, and the easy pair can steal attention from the real question.

The real question is smaller and harder: what job does this choice need to do?

At a fish market before dawn, Claire is buying seafood for a small bistro. Three foam boxes sweat under a hanging scale. The largest looks clean. The middle box is cracked at one corner and badly priced, so the large box feels like the smart upgrade. Claire turns the cracked box backward, counts portions on the chalk board, and sees that the smaller fresh box fits tonight's menu. The comparison frame had been doing more work than the fish.

The limit is important. Comparison is not the enemy. You need comparison because value rarely arrives with a built-in meter. The danger is accepting the nearest comparison as the right one.
breakdown.fullRead:
A decoy is not a bad option by accident. It is a bad option with a job. It stands close enough to a target choice to lose cleanly, and that clean loss makes the target feel safe. The mind likes that feeling. It is easier to say, this one is clearly better than that one, than to ask whether either one belongs in your life.

You see the same move outside retail. A festival volunteer named Nora has a folded program on her knee and three pass choices in front of her. Single-film is cheap. Weekday-only is awkwardly expensive. All-access is only a little more and comes with a red wristband. The all-access pass starts to feel responsible because it dominates the weekday pass. Nora writes the films she can actually attend on the back of the program. Four titles. Two evenings. The wristband stops looking like value and starts looking like a trophy for a schedule she does not have.

That is why the first repair is physical when possible. Hide the decoy. Turn the cracked box around. Cover the weak tier with a receipt. Fold the program over the bad pass. Make the favored option stand without its weaker neighbor.

What if the bigger option still wins after that? Fine. Then it earned the choice on fit, not borrowed contrast.

The deeper trap is that relativity feels like intelligence while it is steering you. You can point to the chart, explain why one plan beats another, and sound perfectly rational. The problem is not the reasoning inside the frame. The problem is that the frame left out the real rivals: your budget, your time, your actual use, the cheaper option that already met the need, or the choice not to buy at all.

At a farm rental counter, Grace studies lift heights during harvest week. The mid-size lift is too short for the upper branches and priced close to the largest model. The biggest machine now looks prudent. Grace steps outside, marks the branch height on the rental-yard fence, and compares that mark with the basic lift's reach. The largest lift had been winning against the wrong opponent.

This also explains why social comparison hurts so cleanly. A nearby salary, kitchen, vacation, or title can become the reference option that grades your life. Nothing about your situation changed. The comparison changed, and satisfaction moved with it.

The defense is not to stop comparing. The defense is to choose the comparison set on purpose. Ask what would compete for the same money, hours, space, or attention if the shiny loser were gone. A clear winner inside the wrong frame can still be the wrong choice.

examples.title: Amelia Covers the Supporter Tier With Her Receipt

planSpec.domain: museum membership desk with one deliberately weak patron tier
planSpec.audience: a museum visitor choosing an annual membership before a family exhibit opens
planSpec.stakes: committing to a donation level that may be steered by a decoy instead of actual visit plans
planSpec.requiredBeat: the visitor covers the middle tier on the laminated rate sheet with a receipt and checks whether the premium tier still looks worth buying

examples.scenario: A laminated membership sheet is clipped to a brass stand beside the coat-check counter. Amelia came for the family pass before the dinosaur exhibit opens, but the patron line has lounge access and the supporter line costs almost as much without guest passes. Her receipt edge hovers over the middle tier. She has to decide whether patron still fits the visits her family will make once that weak tier is covered.
examples.whatToDo: Cover the supporter tier and compare patron against actual visits, guest needs, and budget. Make the premium option win without help from the deliberate loser.
examples.whyItMatters: The supporter tier can steer the choice even if nobody buys it. Removing it forces the patron tier to prove absolute fit instead of winning a rigged contrast.

examples.title: Ben Turns the Cracked Fish Box Around

planSpec.domain: fish market stall comparing catch boxes before dawn
planSpec.audience: a restaurant buyer choosing between seafood boxes under time pressure
planSpec.stakes: overpaying for the largest box because a smaller damaged box makes it look clean
planSpec.requiredBeat: the buyer turns the cracked foam box backward so it cannot act as the loser, then reprices the remaining two boxes by portions served

examples.scenario: Three foam seafood boxes sweat on crushed ice under a hanging scale before dawn. Ben predicts the largest catch box is the safe buy for Friday service because the cracked foam box beside it looks sloppy and overpriced. Before he points to the chalk price board, he must decide whether to turn the cracked box backward and price the remaining boxes by portions served.
examples.whatToDo: Turn the cracked box out of sight, count usable portions, and compare the two real candidates by what the kitchen can sell tonight.
examples.whyItMatters: The cracked box is doing contrast work. Once it stops acting as the loser, the large box has to justify itself against dinner service, not against damage.

examples.title: Nora Writes Four Showtimes on the Program

planSpec.audience: a volunteer choosing between single-film, weekday, and all-access passes
planSpec.stakes: spending a week's food budget because the all-access pass dominates a badly priced weekday pass
planSpec.requiredBeat: the volunteer writes the films they can actually attend on the back of the program before looking at the decoy pass again

examples.scenario: On Saturday afternoon in the festival lobby queue, a folded program rests on Nora's lap, its showtimes circled in pencil beside a red all-access wristband. The weekday-only pass is badly priced, so all-access feels sensible. Nora turns the program over and writes the four films she can actually attend around volunteer shifts and the bus home. The wristband looks different beside those four titles.
examples.whatToDo: Write the real attendance list before choosing. Compare each pass against the films Nora can see, not against a weak weekday-only offer.
examples.whyItMatters: The all-access pass only looks disciplined while the bad pass stands next to it. The schedule exposes whether extra access has real use.

examples.title: Grace Marks the Branch Height on the Fence

planSpec.domain: farm equipment rental counter during harvest week
planSpec.audience: a small orchard owner comparing lift rentals
planSpec.stakes: renting an oversized lift because a useless mid-size option makes it look prudent
planSpec.requiredBeat: the owner steps outside and marks the actual branch height on the rental yard fence before choosing between lifts

examples.scenario: Mud streaks the rental office mat beside a clipboard of lift heights. Grace studies three machines during harvest week. The mid-size lift misses the top branches and costs close to the largest model, so the largest looks prudent. Before signing, she has to decide whether to step outside, mark the branch height on the yard fence, and check which lift reaches the mark.
examples.whatToDo: Use the branch height as the standard. Let the actual orchard need decide the rental instead of letting the useless middle lift make the biggest machine look safe.
examples.whyItMatters: The mid-size lift is a bad reference option. A measured branch height replaces relative dominance with the work the machine must actually do.

examples.title: Martin Hides the Choir Robe Prices

planSpec.audience: a treasurer evaluating fabric packages for a community choir
planSpec.stakes: using donor money on premium trim because the plain-but-overpriced package creates an easy contrast
planSpec.requiredBeat: the treasurer lays the fabric swatches over the price labels and asks which one meets the choir's actual durability rule

examples.scenario: "The premium trim is only a little more," someone says at Thursday's committee meeting in the church basement office. Three fabric swatches are pinned to a felt strip, and Martin sees the plain package is oddly overpriced. Before the committee votes, he must decide whether to lay the swatches over the price labels and ask which fabric meets the durability rule in the donor envelope.
examples.whatToDo: Cover the price labels and test the swatches against durability, cleaning, and donor limits. Let the fabric answer before the weak package creates a winner.
examples.whyItMatters: The premium trim feels responsible only because the plain option was set up to lose. The choir needs robes that last, not a prettier contrast.

examples.title: Sarah Rechecks the Marina Contract After Ignoring the Middle Plan

planSpec.domain: boat storage contract at a winter marina
planSpec.audience: a first-time boat owner choosing storage before the first freeze
planSpec.stakes: buying unnecessary indoor storage because a bad outdoor-plus-service option pushes the premium plan
planSpec.requiredBeat: after ignoring the weak middle contract, the owner measures actual winter access needs against the basic covered rack

examples.scenario: A salt-stiff contract packet flaps under a marina office paperweight. Sarah first circles indoor storage because the outdoor-plus-service plan is expensive and awkward. After ignoring that weak middle contract, she checks winter access hours against the basic covered rack and sees she will visit twice before spring. The indoor plan loses its shine.
examples.whatToDo: Ignore the middle contract and compare covered rack storage against real winter access. Choose by use, not by the plan designed to make indoor storage glow.
examples.whyItMatters: The premium plan borrowed its appeal from a bad neighbor. Once Sarah compares against her own access needs, the storage choice becomes smaller and clearer.

questions.prompt: A manager sees three catering packages: boxed lunch, hot buffet, and hot buffet plus dessert for almost the same price. Nobody would buy the hot buffet alone. What is that middle package doing?
choices: It is acting as a decoy that makes the dessert package look dominant.
It proves the dessert package has the highest absolute value.
It gives the manager a useful average between cheap and premium.
questions.explanation: The middle package is built to lose beside the dessert bundle, so it changes the comparison frame. Absolute value would require checking headcount, appetite, and budget, not just the nearby loser.

questions.prompt: A school librarian must choose between three database licenses. The middle license costs nearly as much as the largest one but lacks archive access. Which move best protects the decision?
choices: Pick the largest license because it beats the middle one clearly.
Hide the middle license and compare the remaining choices against actual student research needs.
Ask the vendor which license most schools choose.
questions.explanation: Hiding the weak middle license tests whether the largest license solves the real research problem. Vendor popularity keeps the seller's frame in charge, and clear dominance over a decoy is not enough.

questions.prompt: A couple touring cabins sees a cramped lake-view unit priced just below a spacious lake-view unit. The spacious one suddenly feels reasonable. What should they do before booking?
choices: Book quickly because lake-view cabins are scarce.
Treat the cramped cabin as proof that lake view is worth the price.
Compare the spacious cabin with their actual plans, including how much time they will spend indoors.
questions.explanation: The cramped cabin may be making the spacious one look better than it is. Their real plans are the missing comparison, while scarcity and lake-view logic both stay inside the planted frame.

questions.prompt: An arts director adds a deliberately weak sponsorship tier before the tier she hopes companies buy. Which risk should she recognize if she wants ethical choice design?
choices: The weak tier may steer buyers by contrast instead of clarifying what each sponsor truly needs.
The weak tier will make all sponsors choose the cheapest package.
The weak tier makes the sponsor list harder to print.
questions.explanation: The ethical risk is steering through a losing comparison. Printing difficulty is irrelevant, and a decoy usually pushes toward the target tier, not toward the cheapest one.

questions.prompt: A person feels worse about a solid apartment after seeing a friend's rooftop pool. Which interpretation best matches relativity?
choices: The apartment became objectively worse once a better one appeared.
A nearby benchmark changed the frame, so satisfaction moved without the apartment changing.
The person should always avoid talking about housing with friends.
questions.explanation: Relativity explains the drop as a benchmark effect: the facts of the apartment did not change. Avoiding all comparison is too broad, and objective quality did not suddenly fall.

questions.prompt: A clinic chooses between two waiting-room chair models after a third, ugly, overpriced model is removed from the catalog. Why might preferences shift?
choices: Removing an ugly option makes people less emotional.
The remaining chairs are now judged without the easy loser that made one seem clearly superior.
Catalog order always determines furniture quality.
questions.explanation: The ugly overpriced chair may have made a target chair look dominant. Once it is gone, people must compare the real candidates directly, which can change the result.

questions.prompt: A city buyer has to choose between three snowplow attachments. One attachment exists mainly to make the premium model look like a bargain. Which question should lead the review?
choices: Which attachment dominates the weakest option most visibly?
Which attachment would look best in the council packet?
Which attachment meets the route, repair, and storage needs if the weak option is ignored?
questions.explanation: The buyer needs to rebuild the choice around route, repair, and storage needs. Dominating the weak option stays inside the decoy frame, and packet appearance is a separate pressure.

questions.prompt: A gym posts three plans, and the annual plan only looks attractive because the monthly-plus-towel plan is absurdly priced. Which action uses the core move best?
choices: Ask whether the annual plan is still attractive when compared with expected visits and cancellation risk.
Choose annual because absurd monthly pricing proves the discount is real.
Choose monthly-plus-towel to avoid being manipulated.
questions.explanation: Expected visits and cancellation risk are the real rivals. Choosing either plan because of the absurd middle option lets the decoy keep control of the frame.

questions.prompt: A buyer says, "I know the premium plan is best because it beats the middle plan on every feature." Which response evaluates the reasoning most accurately?
choices: The reasoning is strong because feature dominance always proves value.
The reasoning is incomplete because the middle plan may be a decoy and the buyer has not tested need or alternatives.
The reasoning is wrong because premium plans are always traps.
questions.explanation: Feature dominance over a weak neighbor is not the same as fit. The buyer still needs to test actual need and alternatives; calling all premium plans traps is just another shortcut.

reviewCards.front: A third option looks bad but makes another option look obviously better. What should you suspect?
reviewCards.back: Suspect a decoy effect. The bad option may exist to lose cleanly so the target option feels safer, larger, or more valuable than it would on its own.

reviewCards.front: You are about to buy the plan that dominates the nearby weaker plan. What is the retrieval move?
reviewCards.back: Remove the weak comparison and rebuild the choice around actual use, budget, and alternatives. If the winner still fits after the decoy disappears, it has a better claim.

reviewCards.front: A friend's upgrade makes your own solid choice feel smaller. What is happening?
reviewCards.back: A nearby benchmark has changed the comparison frame. Relativity can lower satisfaction even when the original choice or situation has not changed at all.

reviewCards.front: A vendor says the premium package is clearly better than the middle package. What question should come next?
reviewCards.back: Ask whether the premium package is better for your real job to be done. Clear superiority over a weak neighbor is not the same as absolute value or practical fit.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Practice frame selection before option selection. The skill is noticing when an easy comparison has become the whole decision, then forcing the choice back onto actual use, cost, time, and alternatives.

ifThenPlans.plan: If one option mainly makes another option look good, then cover it and compare the remaining choice against your original need.
If a vendor presents three tiers, then list the job the tool must do before discussing which tier beats which.
If someone else's upgrade makes your choice feel worse, then write what changed in your facts and what changed only in the benchmark.
If the room keeps praising one option for beating a weak rival, then ask what option or constraint is missing from the comparison set.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Find one three-option choice in front of you, cover the option that seems designed to lose, and write whether the apparent winner still earns its place.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once this week, audit a price sheet, signup list, or proposal menu. Mark any option that looks built to lose, then rebuild the comparison around real use and constraints.

memorableLines.text: The weak option does not need buyers.
memorableLines.why: It compresses the decoy effect into a sentence that is easy to recall at any menu or pricing sheet.

memorableLines.text: A decoy is not a bad option by accident.
memorableLines.why: The line turns a vague suspicion into a concrete design role.

memorableLines.text: A clear winner inside the wrong frame can still be the wrong choice.
memorableLines.why: It names the chapter's central danger without reducing it to generic caution.
